sum: Saputo Inc. produces, markets, and distributes dairy products in Canada, the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom. The company offers mozzarella and cheddar; specialty cheeses, such as ricotta, provolone, parmesan, goat cheese, feta, havarti, snacking, romano, string, blue, and soft and processed cheeses; and brie, camembert, brick, colby, farmer, munster, monterey jack, and fresh curd. It also provides fluid milk, cream, yogurt, sour cream, cottage cheese, and ice cream mixes; and butter and butter blends, flavored cream, dips, half and half, whipping cream, value-added beverages, creamers, coffee beverages, aerosol whipped toppings, almond and oat milk, and aseptic food products and beverages. In addition, the company offers dairy ingredients, including milk powder, whey powder, lactose, and whey protein concentrates, as well as lactoferrin and infant formula; spreads and oils; demineralized whey, lactose, casein, galacto-oligosaccharides, dairy ingredient blends, and nutritional products; and distributes fine imported cheese to specialty stores, and dairy and non-dairy products manufactured by third parties, as well as dairy alternative products. It serves customers in the retail, foodservice, and industrial markets. The company sells its products under the Saputo, Armstrong, Alexis de Portneuf, Bari, Cogruet, DuVillage 1860, Kingsey, Shepherd Gourmet Dairy, Stella, Woolwich Goat Dairy, Dairyland, Neilson, Nutrilait, Baxter, Scotsburn, Trutaste, Milk2Go/Lait's Go, Baileys, Heluva Good, Black Creek, Frigo, Frigo Cheese Heads, Lugano, Montchevre, Mozzeria, Saputo Gold, Treasure Cave, DairyStar, Friendship Dairies, Caboolture, CHEER, Cracker Barrel, Devondale, Great Ocean Road, Liddells, Mersey Valley, Mil Lel, Murray Goulburn Ingredients, Sungold, Tasmanian Heritage, Cathedral City, Clover, Country Life, Davidstow, Frylight, Wensleydale Creamery, Vitalite, and Sheese brands. Saputo Inc. was founded in 1954 and is headquartered in Montreal, Canada.

SAP's Pipeline Problem: Signed Contracts and Shipped Products Still Await Their Revenue Test
sum: SAP has stacked up a series of announcements that, taken at face value, sketch a widening sovereign cloud and artificial intelligence franchise. The harder question for investors is how much of that stack has actually begun producing business — and how much remains a promise with a date attached.

The most concrete commitment is a contract with the Dutch defence ministry covering development and operation of a sovereign cloud environment in the Netherlands. Operations are slated to start on 1 January 2028. That gap matters: a signed agreement underpins the outlook for the offering, but it does not demonstrate a running business. Shareholders would be wrong to treat the deal as realized earnings.

On the product side, SAP said yesterday that "SAP Incentive Management, Starter Edition" is now available. The company and Cohere have also made Cohere North generally available on the SAP Business AI Platform, aimed at regulated industries among others. Here the availability is already a fact — unlike the NTT cooperation announced on 28 October, in which the two firms merely declared their intention to work together on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP Business AI. Their first named area is combining SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site with NTT-managed infrastructure and operations. That division of labour could hand SAP an additional route to delivery, but an announced intent is not a completed collaboration.

The distinction between shipping a product and generating demand from it runs through every one of these items. A live application creates a supply; only customer adoption turns it into a sturdier argument for growth. The same logic applies to the sovereign cloud portfolio, which SAP says targets regulated sectors. If clients in those industries buy both sovereign cloud and AI applications, the two lines could reinforce each other and give SAP several points of contact with a customer rather than dependence on isolated cloud projects. That is a possible development, not a guaranteed business effect.

What would tip the scale is evidence of repeatability — whether SAP can turn individual sovereign cloud engagements into a broader offering. Progress that shows the shift from partnership intent to practical execution would say more than the raw count of new announcements.

AMD shares jump as AI-driven data-center strength fuels growth outlook
sum: AMD, which recently joined the ranks of trillion-dollar companies, has gained about 126% this year and is poised to add about $58 billion in market value if premarket gains hold. The company's strong outlook highlighted growing momentum in its server processor business, signaling that spending on AI computing was extending beyond Nvidia's accelerators, which dominate the market.

"We see demand across the data-center business, across our CPU business, as well as our data-center AI business," CEO Lisa Su said, adding the company had been preparing for that growth for several years.
Su said on Tuesday that the company expects overall revenue to rise more than 80% in 2027, which is higher than the 77% growth analysts estimate, according to LSEG data.

AMD's product roadmap and expanding software ecosystem position it to capture a meaningful share of the AI market, while strengthening its role as the leading alternative to Nvidia and supporting further gains in server CPUs, said analysts at TD Cowen.
Last week, rival Intel's shares plunged more than 20% after the company reported weak PC demand, fueling concerns about its reliance on the PC market and relatively limited exposure to AI.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley are cautious about assuming current growth in the CPU server business will continue indefinitely amid an industry-wide shortage, but they believe AMD is executing better than competitors and could continue to capture a larger share of the market.
The company's third-quarter data-center revenue jumped 97% to $8.55 billion, topping analysts' expectations of $8.20 billion.

Anthropic says revenue surged 1,100% ahead of IPO
sum: Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, on Monday reported a more than 1,100 percent surge in quarterly revenue and nearly $900 billion in spending commitments as it counts down to its Wall Street listing later this month. The filing said the company has committed to spend about $895 billion, mostly on computing power, with $70 billion of that due before September 2027.
The listing comes amid growing nervousness among investors about the huge sums being poured into AI.

Revenue reached $17 billion in the third quarter, up from $1.4 billion a year earlier, though sales growth slowed from previous quarters amid fierce competition from ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and cheaper models, many of them from China.

The company, whose stock market debut is seen as a gauge of how long the AI spending boom lifting the US economy can last, said in an amended filing that its net loss reached $23.3 billion in the July-September period.
The loss stemmed mostly from non-cash accounting charges linked to the company's rising valuation, the filing showed.
Anthropic also posted an operating loss of $567 million in the third quarter as it paid more for short-term computing capacity.

The IPO will be a major test of the market's faith in the AI boom, with the pool of potential investors set to widen as retail traders get their first chance to buy shares directly in a standalone AI giant.

SAP shares climb after Q3 earnings beat and strong cloud revenue outlook
sum: Investing.com -- SAP SE ADRs (NYSE:SAP) rose over 4% in after-hours trading Wednesday after the enterprise software giant delivered third-quarter results that topped Wall Street expectations across key metrics and raised its full-year revenue outlook.

The Germany-based company reported non-IFRS earnings of €1.89 per share on total revenue of €10.27 billion, ahead of analyst estimates pointing to €1.83 per share and €10.10 billion, respectively. Strong demand for enterprise cloud transformations drove a 26% jump in cloud revenue to €6.67 billion, while current cloud backlog expanded 28% to €24.14 billion, reflecting sustained adoption of the company's core software platform.

Against that backdrop, management narrowed its 2026 financial guidance toward the upper bound of previous expectations. SAP now expects full-year cloud revenue to land at the high end of its €25.8 billion to €26.2 billion target range, while maintaining its projection for non-IFRS operating profit between €11.8 billion and €12.2 billion.

The quarter highlighted ongoing operational execution alongside disciplined cost controls as non-IFRS operating profit rose 18% to €3.03 billion, helping offset ongoing declines in legacy software support revenues. Chief Executive Officer Christian Klein noted that enterprise customers are increasingly committing to the company's Business AI offerings and automated tools to drive operational transformations.

Meanwhile, liquidity generation remained strong as free cash flow surged 36% during the quarter to €1.72 billion. The company also continued to return capital to shareholders, repurchasing approximately €4.2 billion worth of shares through the end of September under its multi-year €10 billion buyback program.

SAP's September Patch Surge: A Maximum-Severity Flaw, a Stale Downgrade, and a Stock Drifting 26% Be
sum: SAP pushed out 19 new Security Notes on its September Patch Day, alongside an update to one previously disclosed advisory, addressing 20 vulnerabilities across its product portfolio. The headline item is a memory-corruption flaw in Extended Passport Processing that carries the maximum CVSS rating of 10.0 — tracked as CVE-2026-44756 in separate security reports. A critical kernel gap and a missing-authentication weakness in the NetWeaver Message Server, which could hand attackers system access, round out the most serious findings.

The affected surface is broad: NetWeaver environments, S/4HANA, the Integration Suite, SAPUI5, the ABAP Developer Tools, the NetWeaver Business Client, and Commerce Cloud Search and Navigation all required fixes. For enterprises running SAP systems on-premises or in the cloud, the September cycle translates into fresh patching work — a recurring burden for the software industry at large, but one that lands with particular weight on SAP given the sheer breadth of its customer base. Kernel-level vulnerabilities are especially delicate because they sit deep in the system architecture, and the steady drumbeat of such advisories underscores how large an attack surface SAP's software landscape naturally presents.

Investors took a cautious view. By Thursday the stock was changing hands at EUR 178.16, down 1.1% on the day after closing at EUR 180.18 the previous session — itself a 0.9% decline. Over seven days the shares have shed 4.3%. The weekly slide coincides with the cluster of security warnings, though the more consequential driver for sentiment traces back further.

Late in August, on Wednesday, 26 August, UBS cut its rating on SAP from Buy to Neutral while simultaneously lifting its price target from EUR 164 to EUR 201. The bank pointed to slower-than-expected implementation of customer AI projects and cooling cloud growth. The stock came under pressure in the aftermath, with market watchers also citing broader drags such as oil-price and interest-rate worries. Two weeks on, that downgrade no longer qualifies as a fresh trigger for the current price action.
The longer-term picture is starker. SAP has lost 19% over twelve months and 14% since the start of the year.

For investors, the key comparison is the year-over-year step-up: cloud revenue increased 22% at constant currencies, operating profit increased 26% at constant currencies, and free cash flow increased by EUR 0.88 billion. SAP also said total liabilities were EUR 57.18 billion at 31 December 2025, with cash and cash equivalents at EUR 7.94 billion, which frames the balance-sheet picture around a larger software and cloud base.

That matters more than generic sector optimism because SAP’s own numbers show where growth is coming from and where the backlog is already committed. The comparison between 2024 and 2025 is now visible in revenue, profit, and cash flow, not just in narrative.

SAP Lands a Defense Giant as a Critical Kernel Flaw Tests Investor Patience
sum: SAP's sales machine and its security team delivered contrasting headlines this week. On one side, the Walldorf-based software group secured a marquee win with U.S. defense contractor Lockheed Martin, which will deploy SAP SuccessFactors Solutions to overhaul its HR operations as part of a sweeping workforce transformation. The deal reinforces SAP's standing among large, security-sensitive industrial players that entrust their digital HR backbones to the German vendor.

The Lockheed Martin contract follows hard on the heels of another notable commitment. Just days earlier, German connectivity specialist HARTING said it would accelerate its cloud migration through RISE with SAP. Taken together, the two agreements illustrate how SAP is broadening its cloud and transformation footprint across the spectrum — from mid-sized manufacturers to heavyweights in the defense industry.

The security side of the ledger told a less comfortable story. SAP had already pushed out Security Notes during its regular Patch Day the previous Tuesday. Then on Friday, the SANS security organization flagged an additional, serious vulnerability dubbed "OVERPASS," which affects the SAP kernel during processing of the so-called Extended Passport and carries the highest criticality classification. According to SANS, the disclosure sits within a broader set of 20 vulnerabilities that SAP is addressing in this connection.

That is more than a technical footnote for shareholders. SAP systems sit at the core of countless corporations, and critical kernel flaws routinely stir concerns about potential attack surfaces at existing customers. Clients running S/4HANA, NetWeaver, Integration Suite or Commerce Cloud installations will need to apply the new patches promptly to shield themselves against the flaw rated as critical.

Against the security noise, a signal arrived from inside the company. A member of SAP's executive board purchased 1,500 shares at a price of EUR 178.30 in late August, a transaction worth EUR 267,450. Market watchers often read such insider purchases as a vote of confidence in the company's own strategy, even if they do not, on their own, amount to a buy recommendation.

sum: SAP SE (SAP) moved down by 3.65%. The Software & IT Services sector is down by 1.10%. The company underperformed the industry. Top 3 stocks by turnover in the sector: Salesforce Inc (CRM) down 0.31%; Meta Platforms Inc (META) up 1.32%; Alphabet Inc Class A (GOOGL) down 0.94%.

SAP experienced noticeable downward pressure and intraday volatility as negative market sentiment surrounding the company's artificial intelligence rollout pace and near-term monetization timelines weighed on the stock. Recent Wall Street rating downgrades highlighted execution risks, particularly regarding the deployment speed of SAP's specialized agentic AI tools. Analysts noted that out-of-the-box AI agents across key enterprise workflows are moving slower than initial management targets, raising concerns that corporate clients could look outside the core platform for immediate AI capabilities.

In addition to AI commercialization concerns, investors are digesting expectations of moderating momentum across SAP's cloud segment for the second half of the fiscal year. While core enterprise resource planning demand remains structurally sound, market participants are eyeing a potential deceleration in constant-currency cloud backlog growth. Simultaneously, heavy utilization of migration credits under the company's RISE initiative continues to limit upside potential for near-term free cash flow generation. Profitability expectations have also faced minor headwinds following management's adjustment to full-year operating profit guidance, driven by integration costs and initial dilution from recent software acquisitions alongside higher AI token infrastructure expenses.

Broader sector dynamics and market sentiment have exacerbated trading volatility across the enterprise software landscape. Investors have increasingly heightened their scrutiny on artificial intelligence return timelines, demanding clear revenue contribution rather than strategic projections. Unlike consumer AI applications that achieve rapid adoption, enterprise-grade AI integration requires stringent data governance, regulatory compliance, and complex workflow validation, which naturally lengthens implementation cycles.

SAP's Split Personality: A Downgrade With a Higher Price Target Exposes the Market's Software Nerves
sum: There is a peculiar moment in a stock's life when the ratings agencies and the trading floor seem to be speaking entirely different languages. SAP finds itself in exactly that place this week. The UBS downgrade that arrived on Tuesday carried with it a paradox that sums up the current state of European software investing: the bank cut its recommendation from "Buy" to "Neutral" while simultaneously lifting its price objective from €164 to €201 — a 22 percent increase in the target that somehow still read as bad news to the market.

The logic behind the move, articulated by UBS analyst Michael Briest, was less about the quality of SAP's business and more about the arithmetic of risk and reward. After the stock's recent run, the chance-to-risk profile had simply shifted. When a position has already delivered substantial gains, the marginal value of each additional bet diminishes. That is textbook portfolio management, not a verdict on the company's prospects. Yet the market responded the way markets often do — with selling pressure that had little to do with the underlying fundamentals.

What followed was a sector-wide tremor. Intuit's disappointing revenue guidance for the coming quarter — the US software group projected $23.3 billion to $23.5 billion against market expectations of $23.7 billion — dragged down software valuations across the board. SAP closed Wednesday at €181.04, down 2.2 percent on a day when the entire software complex was under water. The secondary article records a 2.5 percent decline on the day of the downgrade itself, underscoring just how quickly the selling cascaded.

For investors willing to look past the daily noise, the operational picture at Walldorf remains stubbornly robust. The first-half 2026 results, published in early August, showed cloud revenue climbing 24 percent on a currency-adjusted basis to €6.28 billion. The cloud order backlog expanded 26 percent to €22.9 billion. These are not figures that typically accompany sell signals — they describe a company whose multi-year pivot to cloud computing is bearing fruit and whose order books continue to fill.
The tension at the heart of this stock is that the operational story and the trading story have decoupled.

items.t: SAP's €22.9 Billion Cloud Backlog Meets Reality Check as Shares Pause After 20% Surge
sum: The euphoria that swept SAP's stock last week has hit a wall. After a blistering seven-day rally that saw shares climb more than 20%, the German software giant's equity gave back 4.46% on Thursday, settling at €154.98. The pullback comes as investors digest a flurry of analyst revisions and weigh the cost of the company's aggressive artificial intelligence push against its booming cloud business.

The surge that preceded this week's retreat had its roots in second-quarter results released on July 24. Currency-adjusted cloud revenue grew 24%, while the cloud order backlog swelled 27% to €22.9 billion — a figure that handily beat market expectations and set SAP apart from peers struggling to monetize the AI narrative. The performance was enough to propel the stock from deeply oversold territory, with shares gaining 20.14% in a single week.

Yet beneath the headline growth numbers, a more complicated picture emerged. SAP trimmed its full-year operating profit guidance to a range of €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion, down from a previous ceiling of €12.3 billion. The company attributed the revision to dilution from two recent acquisitions: US data platform Dremio, bought in early July, and Freiburg-based AI startup Prior Labs, whose acquisition closed on July 17. SAP plans to invest more than €1 billion in Prior Labs over the next four years, transforming it into a laboratory for structured-data AI — a strategic bet that is weighing on near-term margins.
The operating margin slipped 0.66 percentage points to 27.8%, underscoring the tension between growth and profitability that now defines the SAP investment case.

The market's reassessment played out across a series of analyst notes published this week. Barclays reaffirmed its "Overweight" rating on July 28 but slashed its price target from €255 to €220, explicitly citing margin pressure from the recent M&A spree. Goldman Sachs followed a day later, keeping a "Buy" rating while trimming its target from €230 to €215, though the bank highlighted the robust cloud backlog and strong product pipeline as offsets to short-term margin risk.
JPMorgan struck a more cautious tone, maintaining a "Neutral" stance with a €175 price target and pointing to the second-quarter margin decline despite solid cloud revenues.

sum: German software giant SAP SE (SAP) reported second-quarter cloud revenue growth that exceeded market expectations, driven by the impending expiration of support for its traditional software, while the company also modestly raised its full-year adjusted operating profit guidance.

According to SAP's second-quarter 2026 earnings report released after the U.S. market close on July 23, cloud revenue grew 24% year-over-year on a constant currency basis to €6.28 billion (approximately $7.1 billion), slightly above the Bloomberg-compiled analyst consensus estimate of €6.26 billion. The performance underscores how enterprise customers are being forced to accelerate their migration to the cloud as the 2027 end-of-regular-support deadline for traditional on-premise software approaches.

The earnings report showed SAP's total second-quarter revenue reached €9.88 billion (approximately $11.24 billion), also surpassing analyst expectations of €9.85 billion. Non-IFRS operating profit on a constant currency basis rose 9% year-over-year to €2.81 billion (approximately $3.2 billion). At quarter-end, SAP's current cloud backlog stood at €22.9 billion (approximately $26.05 billion), up 26% on a constant currency basis.

CEO Christian Klein stated in the earnings release: "This performance is underpinned by our Autonomous Enterprise strategy, with our autonomous suite and Business AI Platform maintaining strong momentum. Customers choose SAP to achieve accurate and compliant AI outcomes built on their most critical business processes and data."
Full-Year Profit Guidance Raised, Reflecting Recent Acquisitions

Based on the second-quarter performance, SAP slightly raised its full-year 2026 adjusted operating profit guidance. The company now expects full-year Non-IFRS operating profit on a constant currency basis to be between €11.9 billion and €12.3 billion (approximately $13.54 billion to approximately $13.99 billion), compared to the previous guidance range of €11.8 billion to €12.2 billion.

The guidance increase primarily reflects the dilutive impact of two acquisitions completed earlier this month. SAP acquired Dremio, a high-performance data lakehouse platform, and Prior Labs, a startup focused on developing an AI architecture called Tabular Foundation Models.

sum: Salesforce Inc. CRM shares have declined 5.8% over the past three months, underperforming the Zacks Internet – Software industry's 5.7% gain. While the weak performance may concern investors, Salesforce is far from being the only software stock under pressure.

Several enterprise software names, including SAP SE SAP, Adobe Inc. ADBE and Workiva Inc. WK, have also struggled during the same period. SAP, Adobe and Workiva have fallen 5.1%, 8.7% and 9.9%, respectively. The broad-based weakness suggests that investors are reassessing the software sector rather than losing confidence in Salesforce alone.

The biggest overhang is the rapid rise of artificial intelligence, particularly agentic AI. These AI systems can automate complex business tasks with minimal human intervention, prompting investors to question whether the traditional software-as-a-service (SaaS) pricing model, which largely depends on per-user subscriptions, could face pressure over time. If enterprises eventually require fewer software users, subscription growth could slow across the industry.

At the same time, software companies continue to deal with a difficult macroeconomic backdrop. Higher interest rates, persistent inflation and geopolitical uncertainty have made businesses more cautious about technology spending. Many enterprises are taking longer to approve large software purchases, resulting in extended sales cycles across the industry.

Salesforce is naturally exposed to these trends because most of its revenues come from enterprise customers. Slower IT spending could delay new customer wins and reduce expansion opportunities. However, the recent pullback appears to reflect broader market concerns rather than any meaningful deterioration in Salesforce's business.

Salesforce remains the global leader in customer relationship management software, according to Gartner. However, the company is no longer relying solely on its customer relationship management software for growth. It is transforming into a broader enterprise AI platform by combining customer data, collaboration tools and AI-powered automation.
This strategy has been built through both large and small acquisitions.
